title: The wise men part 1
scripture_text: ‘’After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, during the time of King Herod, Magi from the east came to Jerusalem and asked, “Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews? We saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him.” When King Herod heard this he was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him. When he had called together all the people’s chief priests and teachers of the law, he asked them where the Messiah was to be born. “In Bethlehem in Judea,” they replied, “for this is what the prophet has written: “But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for out of you will come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.’’ Then Herod called the Magi secretly and found out from them the exact time the star had appeared. He sent them to Bethlehem and said, “Go and search carefully for the child. As soon as you find him, report to me, so that I too may go and worship him.” After they had heard the king, they went on their way, and the star they had seen when it rose, went ahead of them until it stopped over the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they were overjoyed. On coming to the house, they saw the child with his mother Mary, and they bowed down and worshipped him. Then they opened their treasures and presented him with gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh. And having been warned in a dream not to go back to Herod, they returned to their country by another route.’’
devotional:
Christmas can be like Marmite, most people love it, but there are some who really hate it. But whether you love it or hate it, (or perhaps you hate what it has become), we can say with some degree of certainty that it is not properly understood.

If you were to ask people what we celebrate at Christmas, many would rightly say that we celebrate the birth of Jesus. However, if you were to ask, ‘what are the implications of Jesus’ birth? Or how should it, or how has it affected or changed their lives?, we would probably get a lot of questioning looks!!!

A lot of people are inclined to think about Christmas in the same way as they would view a Hans Christian Anderson story. It has a kind of ‘fairytale’ feel about it. However, when you tear away all they myths and misunderstandings that surrounds the Christmas story, we discover a story that will perhaps disturb, challenge and expose the priorities by which we have chosen to live.

When we turn to the New Testament and try to grasp what really happened, we will discover that the story of Jesus’ birth exposes what kind of relationship we have with him. Christmas is an opportunity for us to ask ourselves ‘How am I treating Jesus?’ Perhaps we have turned the Christmas story into a fairytale which doesn’t make any demands of us, (except financially) nor does it challenge our thinking?

So as we unpack this part of the Christmas story, we are going to examine how we are relating to Jesus in the here and now.

As we go through our passage we need to ask ourselves, ‘what kind of relationship do I have with Jesus’?

Everyone of us relates to Jesus in some way. No matter who we are, we all have an opinion about Jesus, and we have all decided what kind of relationship we want with him. Hopefully as we look at the people in this part of the Christmas story and how they related to Jesus, we will be able to see who we best identify with, and see what we can change so we can discover the great honour of loving Jesus more.

1. Herod.

He was threatened by Jesus.

Matthew places the birth of Jesus in a political context, Matthew wants his readers to see that Jesus as King. So in chapter 2 he introduces Jesus as king of the Jews. When Herod heard this he was deeply disturbed. The word Matthew uses to describe Herod's emotions means to be 'deeply disturbed' Greek word tarassō, this was a very emotional word, which carries the idea of acute mental distress, disquiet, to make restless, it literally means to shake back and forth. So what is going on here?

Let me tell you a few things about Herod. He was named King of the Jews by the Roman Senate in 40 B. C. By 37 B. C. he had crushed, with the help of Roman forces, all opposition to his rule. He was wealthy, politically gifted, intensely loyal, an excellent administrator, and clever enough to remain in the good graces of successive Roman emperors. His famine relief was superb and his building projects (including the temple, begun 20 B.C.) were admired even by his foes.

But he loved power, he inflicted incredibly heavy taxes on the people, and resented the fact that many Jews considered him a usurper. In his last years, suffering an illness that compounded his paranoia, he turned to cruelty and in fits of rage and jealousy killed close associates, his wife Marianne and at least two of his sons. Caesar once said it was better to be Herod’s pig than his son.

Here is the point, Herod understood that if Jesus was born King of the Jews, then he could not be King of the Jews, so his control, power and position was threatened. He was terrified of not being in control. For him power and position were essential, so he would go to any length to protect his throne and kingdom.

We might not like to admit it, but there is something of Herod in all of us. We may not be cruel like him, but we want to be in control, we want to be king of our lives.

However, the message of Christmas is, ‘You cannot be king/queen, you cannot be in control.’ The message of Christmas is that Jesus is King, not me, not you.

Like Herod we develop subtle and almost in-perceptible ways of holding onto our thrones.
prayer: Father thank you that Jesus birth reminds us that He is King.
